questions.text: Why can Monte Carlo policy evaluation work without knowing the environment’s transition probabilities?

options.A: It solves the Bellman equation by enumerating every possible next state.
options.B: It averages returns observed after visits to states in sampled episodes.
options.C: It replaces environment transitions with a learned dynamics model.
options.D: It chooses only greedy actions, so all transitions become predictable.

questions.explanation: Monte Carlo estimates expected return by sampling whole episodes and averaging observed returns; it need not enumerate or know transition probabilities.

questions.text: A Monte Carlo evaluator runs a policy in an environment where some episodes can loop indefinitely. What practical change lets it collect bounded rollouts while making the truncation explicit?

options.A: Use an unlimited rollout and wait for every trajectory to finish naturally.
options.B: Stop after a maximum step count and report capped episodes separately.
options.C: Replace observed returns with exact Bellman expectations from a model.
options.D: Treat every incomplete trajectory as a successful terminal episode.

questions.explanation: Monte Carlo needs bounded episodes for usable returns. A max-step cap prevents endless rollouts, and tracking capped episodes makes the resulting truncation visible.

questions.text: A state starts with V=2 and has count=3. The next first-visit return is G=6. After counts[s] += 1 and V[s] += (G−V[s])/counts[s], what is the new V?
questions.explanation: The new count is 4, so the incremental update is 2 + (6−2)/4 = 3.
